pos: n. (the Loire town whose Reformed academy, founded in 1593, became the school of hypothetical universalism)
etymology: French Saumur, from a Gallo-Roman or Frankish settlement name; the town stands on the Loire in Anjou.
biblical_def: Saumur is the Loire town whose academy was the most learned and the most troublesome of the French Reformed schools. Philippe Duplessis-Mornay, Huguenot statesman and governor of the town, founded it in 1593 as a Protestant university for the western provinces, and it drew the best men in France and some from abroad. John Cameron, a Scot, taught there and framed a scheme in which God wills the salvation of all men on condition of faith, and then wills effectually the faith of the elect. Moise Amyraut, his pupil and from 1633 the academy's principal, published this as a universal conditional decree preceding election; Paul Testard taught the same at Blois; Josue de la Place denied the immediate imputation of Adam's sin, which the national synod of Charenton condemned in 1645; and Louis Cappel demonstrated that the Hebrew vowel points are a later addition, which was true and was received as an attack on the text's authority. The synod of Alencon in 1637 examined Amyraut and did not condemn him; the Helvetic Consensus Formula of 1675 was written by the Swiss against the whole Saumur school. The dictionary enters Saumur because it is the clearest case of a genuinely devout faculty that softened the doctrines of grace by degrees, and of a church that could not bring itself to say so.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a decree as an established law or purpose; imputation as the reckoning of something to a person; a vowel point as a mark denoting a vowel sound; and a formula as a prescribed form of words.
webster_full: DECREE, n. Judicial decision; an edict or law; in theology, the predetermined purpose of God.
IMPUTATION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution; the reckoning of anything to a person.
VOWEL, n. A simple sound formed by the continuous passage of the breath; a letter representing such a sound.
FORMULA, n. A prescribed form; a rule or model; a stated form of words in which anything is expressed.
CONDITION, n. That which is established or determined as a requisite to the performance of something else.
scriptures: According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
corruption_summary: Loire town whose Reformed academy, founded by Duplessis-Mornay in 1593, taught the hypothetical universalism of Cameron and Amyraut against which the Helvetic Consensus was framed in 1675.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the conditional universal decree, and the dictionary names it as a softening of election rather than a harmless refinement of it. Saumur taught a first decree to save all men if they believe, with the effectual decree following; Scripture puts the choosing first and makes it particular, for he “hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4), and the chain that follows admits no conditional stage: “whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified” (Rom 8:30). De la Place's denial of the immediate imputation of Adam's sin was condemned at Charenton in 1645, and the ground of the condemnation is that “by one man's disobedience many were made sinners” is the parallel on which justification itself rests.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the certainty of the covenant transaction between the Father and the Son, which a conditional decree makes uncertain. “All that the Father giveth me shall come to me” (Joh 6:37) is a promise of completed success, and the imputation on which the whole structure stands is stated plainly: “by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19). The dictionary records that Amyraut was pious, learned and a loyal son of the French church, and that Cappel's work on the vowel points was sound scholarship wrongly feared, and that neither fact alters the verdict on the decree.

pos: n. (the Bearnais town whose academy Jeanne d'Albret founded in 1566 to train a Reformed ministry for the Pyrenees)
etymology: French Orthez, Bearnais Ortes, from a Basque or Gascon root; the old capital of the viscounts of Bearn on the Gave de Pau.
biblical_def: Orthez is the Bearnais town where the Reformed religion of a small Pyrenean state was given a school to live on. Jeanne d'Albret, having established the Reformation in Bearn by ordinance, founded an academy there in 1566, endowing it out of the confiscated revenues of the abbeys and chapters, with chairs of theology, Hebrew, Greek and philosophy, and the plain object of training Bearnais and Basque-speaking ministers for Bearnais and Basque-speaking parishes rather than importing Frenchmen from Geneva. Lambert Daneau and other men of standing taught there, students came from Gascony and Navarre as well as Bearn, and the academy was later moved to Lescar. It worked for half a century and ended abruptly: Louis XIII's expedition of 1620 reduced Bearn, restored the Catholic church and the chapters' revenues, and the academy did not survive the restoration. The dictionary enters Orthez because the question a reforming prince faces is not whether to decree but whether to endow, and a school paid for out of the old church's revenues and set to train men in the local languages is the right answer to it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to endow as to furnish with a permanent fund; a chapter as the body of clergy of a cathedral; a chair as a professorship; and revenue as income from property.
webster_full: ENDOW, v. To furnish with a portion of estate; to settle a permanent provision upon, as a college or church.
CHAPTER, n. The body of clergy belonging to a cathedral or collegiate church; an assembly of monks.
CHAIR, n. A seat of justice or of authority; a professorship in a university.
REVENUE, n. The annual rents, profits, interest or issues of any species of property; income.
ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
corruption_summary: Bearnais town whose academy, founded and endowed by Jeanne d'Albret in 1566, trained Bearnais and Basque-speaking ministers until the French reduction of 1620.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the reformation that decrees and does not pay. A prince can abolish the mass by proclamation in a morning; the ministers who must then preach every Sunday for forty years in the valleys have to be found, taught, examined and maintained, and that costs money and a building. Jeanne d'Albret turned the abbeys' revenues to exactly that use, which is the apostolic order: elders who labour in the word are to be counted “worthy of double honour” (1Ti 5:17), and what was left wanting is to be set in order and elders ordained “in every city” (Tit 1:5).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the training of local men for local speech. Orthez existed so that a Bearnais parish would not be served by a Frenchman reading French to people who thought in Bearnais or Basque, which is the Pentecostal rule applied to a seminary: men hear “in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8). The handing on is the apostolic charge itself, that what has been heard be committed “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2), and the academy did that for half a century before an army ended it.

pos: n. (the Loire chateau of the Estates-General of 1576 and 1588, where Henry III had the duke of Guise murdered)
etymology: French Blois, from a Gallic or Gallo-Roman root Blesum; the town and royal chateau stand on the Loire between Orleans and Tours.
biblical_def: Blois is the royal chateau on the Loire where the French crown resolved its quarrel with the Catholic League by assassination. Henry III summoned the Estates-General there in 1576, which pressed him to suppress the Reformed religion, and again in 1588, by which time Henry, duke of Guise, head of the League and effective master of Paris, had driven the king out of his own capital and was dictating terms. On the morning of 23 December 1588 the king had Guise summoned to his chamber and killed in the antechamber by his own guards, the Forty-Five, with daggers; the cardinal of Guise was murdered in the castle the next day. France was thrown into open civil war against its king, Henry III was himself assassinated by the friar Jacques Clement eight months later, and the crown passed to the Protestant Henry of Navarre. Blois also had a Reformed congregation and gave the academy of Saumur its teacher Paul Testard. The dictionary enters Blois because it is the Catholic League's mirror of Orleans: there a Protestant gentleman shot a Catholic duke, here a Catholic king had a Catholic duke stabbed, and the dictionary applies the same commandment to both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chateau as a castle or country seat; an antechamber as a chamber leading to a chief apartment; a league as a confederacy; and regicide as the murder of a king.
webster_full: CHATEAU, n. A castle; a house in the country; a gentleman's country seat.
ANTECHAMBER, n. A chamber or apartment before the chief apartment, where persons wait for audience.
LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.
REGICIDE, n. A king-killer; one who murders a king; the murder of a king.
DAGGER, n. A short sword; a poniard; an instrument of stabbing.
scriptures: A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood,
Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
corruption_summary: Loire chateau of the Estates-General of 1576 and 1588, where Henry III had the duke of Guise stabbed on 23 December 1588 and was himself murdered eight months later.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is political murder treated as statecraft, and Blois is where a king practised it in his own house. Guise was a dangerous man who had broken his oath and seized his sovereign's capital, and none of that gave a king the right to have him stabbed by guards in an antechamber instead of tried. The commandment is unqualified, “Thou shalt not kill” (Exo 20:13), and the proverb names what the Lord hates in such a scene: “hands that shed innocent blood” (Pro 6:17) in a court where the forms of law were available and not used.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the magistrate is as much under the law as the subject, and that blood shed outside its forms returns on the shedder. The ordinance given to Noah is the ground of all civil justice and also its limit: “Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed” (Gen 9:6), which establishes a court rather than a dagger. Within eight months Henry III was knifed by a friar in his own camp, and “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52) was fulfilled on the man who had used it first.

pos: n. (the Dordogne town of the peace of 1577, a Huguenot place of surety whose walls were pulled down in 1621)
etymology: French Bergerac, from a Gallo-Roman estate name with the suffix -acum; the town stands on the Dordogne in Perigord.
biblical_def: Bergerac is the Dordogne town that shows what the Huguenot settlement actually consisted of. A river port in Perigord with a Reformed majority from the 1560s, it held a college, printed books, and was one of the places of surety, the fortified towns the crown conceded to the Protestants as a guarantee that the edicts of pacification would be kept. The sixth religious war ended there: negotiations at Bergerac in September 1577 produced the terms published as the Edict of Poitiers, which restored Reformed worship under limits and confirmed a reduced list of garrison towns. The arrangement was never stable, because it made the Reformed church a party with fortresses and gave the crown a permanent grievance; Louis XIII and Richelieu set about removing the places of surety one by one, and in 1621 Bergerac submitted and had its walls and towers demolished. By the Peace of Alais in 1629 the Huguenots kept their religion and lost every stronghold, which left them wholly dependent on a royal promise, and the promise was revoked in 1685. The dictionary enters Bergerac because a church with walls is tempted to trust them, and because losing them was in one sense a mercy and in another the beginning of the end.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines surety as security against loss; a garrison as troops stationed in a fort; to demolish as to pull down a structure; and pacification as the act of making peace.
webster_full: SURETY, n. Certainty; indubitableness; security against loss or damage; a pledge or hostage.
GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town to defend it against an enemy.
DEMOLISH, v. To throw or pull down; to raze; to destroy, as a heap or structure.
PACIFICATION, n. The act of making peace between parties at variance; the act of appeasing.
RAMPART, n. An elevation or wall of earth round a place, capable of resisting the force of cannon.
scriptures: The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
corruption_summary: Dordogne town where the sixth religious war was settled in September 1577, a Huguenot place of surety whose walls were demolished in 1621.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the church that trusts a fortress and a treaty. The places of surety were a reasonable precaution after 1572 and the dictionary does not call them sinful; it records what they did to the French Reformed church, which was to make it a political party with garrisons, give every king a reason to besiege it, and teach its people to reckon their safety in walls. The prophet's word is the exact diagnosis: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5), and the walls came down in 1621 whatever had been promised in 1577.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is where a church's security actually lies. “except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1) was true of Bergerac's ramparts, and the alternative is stated plainly: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). The tower that does hold is named in the proverb, that “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10), and after 1629 the Huguenots had no other.

pos: n. (the Albret court town that sheltered the first French evangelicals and became Jeanne d'Albret's Reformed capital)
etymology: French Nérac, from a Gallo-Roman estate name with the suffix -acum; the chateau of the Albrets stands on the Baise in Gascony.
biblical_def: Nerac is the small Gascon court town that twice sheltered the French Reformation at the moment it had nowhere else to go. Marguerite of Navarre, sister of Francis I, held her court there and at Pau, and in the 1530s and 1540s she used her rank to protect the first French evangelicals when the Parlement of Paris was burning them: Jacques Lefevre d'Etaples, the translator of the French Bible, spent his last years at Nerac under her protection and died there about 1536; Gerard Roussel, Clement Marot and others of the Meaux circle found refuge; and the young Calvin is said to have visited Lefevre there. Marguerite herself never left the Roman church, and the dictionary records that her theology was a reforming Catholic mysticism rather than the Reformed faith, and that her protection was real and saved lives. Her daughter Jeanne d'Albret went further and made Nerac the Reformed capital of her sovereignty. The conference of Nerac in 1578 and 1579, between Catherine de Medici and the king of Navarre, produced the Edict of Nerac adjusting the places of surety. The dictionary enters Nerac because the French Reformation's first decade survived on the protection of a princess who did not share its doctrine.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines protection as the act of defending from evil; a court as the residence of a sovereign; refuge as shelter from danger; and mysticism as obscure religious sentiment.
webster_full: PROTECTION, n. The act of protecting; defense; shelter from evil; preservation from loss or injury.
COURT, n. The place where a sovereign resides; the hall or chamber where justice is administered.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects.
MYSTICISM, n. Obscurity of doctrine; the doctrine of the Mystics, who profess a pure, sublime and perfect devotion.
PRINCESS, n. A female sovereign; the daughter of a king; the consort of a prince.
scriptures: Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.
Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.
Because I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him.
If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain;
corruption_summary: Gascon court town where Marguerite of Navarre sheltered Lefevre d'Etaples and the Meaux circle, and which Jeanne d'Albret made her Reformed capital.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the demand that a protector be sound before his protection is honoured. Marguerite of Navarre was not a Reformed believer; she stayed in the Roman church, wrote mystical verse the dictionary does not commend, and sheltered men whom the Parlement of Paris would have burned. The dictionary states both and refuses to diminish the second for the sake of the first. What she did is what Scripture commands of anyone with power: “Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction” (Pro 31:8).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of rescue laid on those in a position to perform it. “If thou forbear to deliver them that are drawn unto death” (Pro 24:11) is a warning addressed to the bystander, and the question put to Esther is the same question put to a princess at a hostile court: “who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Est 4:14). Of a man who used his standing this way Job could say, “I delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him” (Job 29:12), and that is what Nerac was for about fifteen years.

pos: n. (the Rhone city of Waldo and the Poor Men of Lyons, a great printing centre, and the scene of the massacre of 1572)
etymology: French Lyon, from Latin Lugdunum, the fort of Lugus or of the raven; the city stands where the Saone joins the Rhone.
biblical_def: Lyon is the French city where the longest-lived medieval reforming movement began. About 1173 a rich merchant of Lyons, known as Waldo, gave away his goods, commissioned a translation of the Gospels and other Scripture into the vernacular, and began to preach in the streets; his followers, the Poor Men of Lyons, were forbidden to preach by the archbishop, appealed to Rome, were refused at the Third Lateran Council in 1179, continued anyway, and were excommunicated at Verona in 1184. From that excommunication came the Waldenses of the Alps, who kept their own preachers and vernacular Scriptures for three and a half centuries and joined the Reformation at Chanforan in 1532. Lyon was also one of Europe's great printing cities and a crossroads for books from Geneva, and it held a large Reformed congregation; the Protestants took control of the city in 1562 under the Baron des Adrets, whose reprisals against Catholic prisoners the dictionary names as atrocities, and in the last days of August 1572 the city's Protestants were massacred in the wake of the Paris killings, some seven or eight hundred being murdered, many in the prisons, in what is called the Vespers of Lyon. The dictionary enters Lyon because the whole Waldensian line begins with one merchant who wanted Scripture in French.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a merchant as one who traffics on a large scale; to excommunicate as to expel from the communion of the church; a vespers as the evening service; and a reprisal as the seizing of what belongs to another in retaliation.
webster_full: MERCHANT, n. A man who trafficks or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who exports and imports goods.
EXCOMMUNICATE, v. To expel from communion; to eject from the communion of the church by an ecclesiastical sentence.
VESPERS, n. The evening song or service in the Roman Catholic church.
REPRISAL, n. The act of taking from an enemy by way of retaliation or indemnity for something taken or withheld.
POVERTY, n. Destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence.
scriptures: Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me.
For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
corruption_summary: Rhone city where Waldo and the Poor Men of Lyons began preaching about 1173, a great printing centre, and the scene of the massacre of some seven hundred Protestants in 1572.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the prohibition of lay preaching, which is how the Waldensian movement was created. Waldo and his companions were not condemned at first for heresy but for preaching without licence; they had Scripture in their own tongue and would not stop speaking from it, and the sentence of Verona in 1184 made a separated church out of men who had asked permission to stay. The apostolic answer to the identical order was given before the Sanhedrin: “we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20), and the ground of it was that “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a man who gives up his goods to preach is doing a thing Scripture commends, and the Lord's word to the rich young man is the text Waldo acted on: “go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven” (Mat 19:21). The dictionary records the other side of Lyon's history without softening it: the Baron des Adrets's reprisals in 1562 were murder done by our side, and the seven hundred killed in the prisons in 1572 are of those “slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9).

pos: n. (the Norman capital whose Reformed cloth trade was broken by the Revocation and carried to Norwich and Spitalfields)
etymology: French Rouen, from Latin Rotomagus, the market of the wheel or of Roto; the city stands on the Seine below Paris.
biblical_def: Rouen is the Norman capital whose Protestant population was large, industrial and in the end exported. The city held one of the biggest Reformed congregations in France, concentrated among its cloth merchants, dyers, weavers and printers; it was taken by the Reformed in 1562 and retaken by the crown with a sack, and it suffered prison massacres in September 1572 after the Paris killings. Under the Edict of Nantes it had a temple outside the walls at Quevilly and a share in the Chambre de l'Edit, the mixed court at Paris that heard Protestant cases. The Revocation of 1685 fell on Rouen as an industrial event. Emigration was forbidden on pain of the galleys, and the Protestants of Rouen left anyway in thousands, taking their skills with them: the new-draperies of Norwich, the silk weaving of Spitalfields in London, and workshops in Holland and Brandenburg were built on French artisans, many of them from Normandy, and the trade of Rouen did not recover for generations. Elie Benoist, pastor at Alencon, wrote the history of the whole business from exile in Delft. The dictionary enters Rouen because the Revocation is usually counted in souls and should also be counted in looms, since the king who drove them out impoverished himself to do it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a draper as one who deals in cloth; a loom as a frame for weaving; emigration as removal from one country to another; and a galley as a vessel rowed by convicts.
webster_full: DRAPER, n. One who sells cloths; a dealer in cloths; as a linen draper or woolen draper.
LOOM, n. A frame or machine of wood or other material, in which a weaver works threads into cloth.
EMIGRATION, n. Removal of inhabitants from one country or state to another, for the purpose of residence.
GALLEY, n. A low flat-built vessel navigated with sails and oars, often rowed by criminals condemned to it.
ARTISAN, n. One trained to manual dexterity in some mechanic art or trade; a handicraftsman.
scriptures: And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;

And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles.
Now they which were scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch, preaching the word to none but unto the Jews only.
corruption_summary: Norman capital whose large Reformed artisan population was massacred in 1572 and, after the Revocation of 1685, emigrated to Norwich, Spitalfields, Holland and Brandenburg.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the state that believes it can take a man's religion and keep his trade. Louis XIV revoked the Edict, forbade emigration on pain of the galleys, and expected the Huguenot weavers of Rouen to attend mass and go on weaving; perhaps two hundred thousand left the kingdom, and the skills left with them. The dictionary records this not as a providential joke but as the plain working of a moral order: a crown that treats conscience as a commodity will find that it has valued the commodity wrongly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of a trade pursued as a calling, which is what these congregations were made of. Paul lodged with Aquila and Priscilla and worked, “for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3), and the apostolic charge to a congregation of artisans is to “work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11). What happened to Rouen is what happened at Jerusalem, that after a great persecution “they were all scattered abroad” (Act 8:1), and the scattered “travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch” (Act 11:19), which for Normans meant Norwich, London and Berlin.

“they were all scattered abroad” (Act 8:1) — the Revocation of 1685 and emigration on pain of the galleys.
“and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) — the looms of Norwich and Spitalfields.

pos: n. (the Loire city of the silk weavers, whose Protestants were drowned in the river in 1562)
etymology: French Tours, from the Turones, the Gallic people of the region; Latin Caesarodunum and later Turonum.
biblical_def: Tours is the Loire city whose Reformed congregation was drowned. Royal favour had planted a silk industry there in the fifteenth century, and by the 1550s a large part of the weavers, dyers and small masters of the trade were Reformed, as the artisan classes of the French towns generally were; Tours also housed royal officials and a wealthy legal class that mostly was not. In July 1562, at the opening of the first religious war, the Catholic party took control of the city and killed the Protestants in numbers, a great many of them being bound and thrown into the Loire over several days, with estimates in the hundreds; the massacre at Tours is one of the earliest and least remembered of the series that runs through Sens, Orange and Vassy to Paris in 1572. The dictionary enters Tours because the French religious wars are generally recounted as battles between noble factions, and the people who actually died in them were town artisans killed by their neighbours in weeks when no army was present; and because the Loire, which carried the barges of a prosperous trade, was used for this.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a weaver as one who makes cloth; a dyer as one who colours cloth; to drown as to deprive of life by immersion; and a faction as a party in political society.
webster_full: WEAVER, n. One whose occupation is to weave; one who makes cloth or other textile fabric.
DYER, n. One whose occupation is to dye cloth and the like; one who colours stuffs.
DROWN, v. To deprive of life by immersion in water or other fluid; to overwhelm in water.
FACTION, n. A party, in political society, combined or acting in union, in opposition to the government.
ARTISAN, n. One trained to manual dexterity in some mechanic art or trade; a handicraftsman.
scriptures: I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me.
Then the waters had overwhelmed us, the stream had gone over our soul:

When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
corruption_summary: Loire city of the silk trade whose Reformed weavers and artisans were killed in July 1562, many bound and thrown into the river.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the massacre done by neighbours rather than by armies, which is what most of the French religious wars consisted of for the people who died in them. At Tours in July 1562 there was no battle; the Catholic faction took the town, and weavers and dyers who had lived beside their killers for years were bound and put into the Loire. The dictionary names it murder, names that it was done by the Catholic party in this instance, and records that the Reformed did comparable things at Orange and in the Dauphine in the same months.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the psalmist's language for being overwhelmed, which these people had reason to use literally. “I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me” (Psa 69:2) is a figure for distress that at Tours was not a figure, and the psalm of deliverance says “Then the waters had overwhelmed us, the stream had gone over our soul” (Psa 124:4). The promise given is not of exemption but of presence: “When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee” (Isa 43:2). Their cry is the one under the altar, “How long, O Lord, holy and true” (Rev 6:10).

“Then the waters had overwhelmed us, the stream had gone over our soul” (Psa 124:4) — a massacre with no army present.
“When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee” (Isa 43:2) — weavers killed by their own neighbours.

pos: n. (the Garonne city whose College de Guyenne taught Buchanan and Montaigne, and whose Protestants were massacred in October 1572)
etymology: French Bordeaux, from Latin Burdigala, of Aquitanian origin; the city stands on the Garonne above its estuary.
biblical_def: Bordeaux is the Garonne city where Renaissance learning and the Reformation met in one school and then parted. The College de Guyenne, founded by the city in 1533, became for a generation the best school in France: Andre de Gouvea ran it, and its masters included the Scot George Buchanan, later tutor to James VI and the ablest Latinist of the age, and Elie Vinet; Michel de Montaigne was a pupil, Latin-speaking from infancy by his father's arrangement. Several of its masters were suspected of Lutheran opinions and some fled; Buchanan was afterwards tried by the Portuguese inquisition. The city itself held a Reformed congregation, a Parlement that persecuted it, and a strong royal and Catholic interest; in October 1572, some weeks after the Paris massacre, the Protestants of Bordeaux were killed in numbers on the initiative of the local authorities and the Jesuit preacher Edmond Auger, with estimates of several hundred dead. The dictionary enters Bordeaux because its college shows how close the new learning came to the Reformation without becoming it, Montaigne going the way of a sceptical quiet Catholicism and Buchanan the way of the Scottish Kirk out of the same classroom.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a college as a society for learning; a Latinist as one skilled in Latin; scepticism as doubt of the truth of religion; and an inquisition as a court for the trial of heretics.
webster_full: COLLEGE, n. A society of men invested with certain powers, engaged in some common pursuit, chiefly of learning.
LATINIST, n. One skilled in Latin; one versed in the Latin language and its authors.
SCEPTICISM, n. Doubt; a doubting; the doctrine that no facts can be certainly known; universal doubt.
INQUISITION, n. A court in some Roman Catholic countries for the examination and punishment of heretics.
TUTOR, n. One who has the care of instructing another in various branches of learning.
scriptures: For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe.
Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
corruption_summary: Garonne city whose College de Guyenne taught Buchanan and Montaigne from 1533, and whose Protestants were massacred in October 1572.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is learning that never arrives anywhere, which the Bordeaux college produced as readily as it produced reformers. The same classrooms sent out George Buchanan, who became a Reformed polemicist and the tutor of a king, and Michel de Montaigne, whose essays are among the most agreeable books ever written and whose conclusion was a cultivated suspension of judgement. The apostle has the measure of the second: men “Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2Ti 3:7). The dictionary values the learning highly and declines to confuse it with faith.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of knowing, in which reverence comes first: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Pro 1:7). Scholarship without that is addressed by the warning that “Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” (1Co 8:1), and by the plain statement that God chose another instrument, since “the world by wisdom knew not God” (1Co 1:21). The dictionary records the city's other half as well: several hundred of its Protestants were killed in October 1572 while a Jesuit preached.

“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Pro 1:7) — the College de Guyenne founded in 1533.
“the world by wisdom knew not God” (1Co 1:21) — several hundred killed at Bordeaux in October 1572.

pos: n. (the Garonne town of the Huguenot potter Bernard Palissy, who was imprisoned for the gospel and died in the Bastille)
etymology: French Agen, from Latin Aginnum, of Gallic origin; the town stands on the Garonne between Bordeaux and Toulouse.
biblical_def: Agen is the Garonne town where a working potter became one of the Reformation's most unusual confessors. Bernard Palissy, born near Agen about 1510, was a glass-painter and surveyor who spent sixteen years in poverty teaching himself to make enamelled earthenware, burning his own furniture to fire his kilns, and succeeded: his rustic ware, moulded with fish, lizards and shells cast from life, made him famous and eventually got him a royal appointment and lodgings in the Tuileries. He was also a self-taught natural philosopher who lectured in Paris on springs, fossils and agriculture, and argued from the fossil shells of the Ardennes that they were the remains of real creatures, which the schools of his day denied. And he was a Reformed Protestant from the 1540s. He was imprisoned at Bordeaux in 1562 and saved only by the intervention of the constable Montmorency, who wanted his pottery; he was arrested again as an old man after the League took Paris, refused to recant, was condemned, and died in the Bastille about 1590 in his eightieth year. The dictionary enters Agen because Palissy is what the Reformation looked like in a workshop, and because he was offered his liberty for a word and did not say it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a potter as one who makes earthen vessels; enamel as a substance of the nature of glass; a kiln as a furnace for baking; and a fossil as a substance dug out of the earth.
webster_full: POTTER, n. One whose occupation is to make earthen vessels; one who makes pots.
ENAMEL, n. A substance of the nature of glass, differing from it by a greater degree of fusibility or opacity.
KILN, n. A fabric of brick or stone, which may be heated for the purpose of hardening, burning or drying.
FOSSIL, n. A substance dug out of the earth; in modern usage, the petrified remains of animals or plants.
RECANT, v. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to unsay what has been said.
scriptures: O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel.
But now, O LORD, thou art our father; we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand.
But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
corruption_summary: Garonne town where the Huguenot potter Bernard Palissy was born about 1510, who refused to recant and died in the Bastille about 1590.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the recantation bought with a man's craft. Palissy was useful: a constable saved him from a Bordeaux prison in 1562 because the king's works wanted his enamels, and at the end he was offered his life for a word and refused it at nearly eighty. The dictionary records that he was spared once for his usefulness and killed at last for his confession, and that the second is the measure of the man. “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32) is what he acted on in the Bastille.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the figure a potter's whole life was lived inside. “Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand” (Jer 18:6) is said to a nation, and the prophet's confession is the creature's proper answer: “we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand” (Isa 64:8). Palissy made vessels for kings and was himself one of the vessels the apostle describes, for “we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God” (2Co 4:7).

Greek ostrakinos (G3749) — made of earthenware, of baked clay; “we have this treasure in earthen vessels”, 2 Corinthians 4:7.
Greek homologeo (G3670) — to confess, to say the same thing; “shall confess me before men”, Matthew 10:32.

“we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2Co 4:7) — a potter spared in 1562 because his work was wanted.
“shall confess me before men” (Mat 10:32) — condemned at nearly eighty and dead in the Bastille about 1590.
